Publish a supplement site

Source: vignettes/publishing.Rmd
publishing.Rmd

This guide takes you from an empty folder to a published site. GitHub Pages serves the site, and Zenodo archives each GitHub release with a DOI. You do each step once, in this order. The last part gives the rule for rendering again after you change a report.

The code blocks run in two places. Run each r block in the R console. Run each sh block in a terminal, such as the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron. Each step names the folder to run its commands in. To run R in the site folder, start R there or open the folder as a project. You can also run setwd() with the path of the folder.

1. Find missing tools

In the R console, in any folder, install the package and list the tools:

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("jmgirard/supplement")
supplement::check_tools()

check_tools() reports whether Quarto, knitr, rmarkdown, git, and the GitHub command-line tool (gh) are installed. Install each tool that it reports as missing or too old. If it reports Quarto as not on the system path, add Quarto’s bin folder to the path. It also reminds you of the two accounts that you need: a GitHub account and a Zenodo account.

2. Make the GitHub repository and clone it

On GitHub, make a new public repository. Do not add a README, a .gitignore, or a license. The template writes those files.

In a terminal, in the folder that will hold the site folder, clone the repository. Use your GitHub user name for owner and the repository’s name for name:

git clone https://github.com/owner/name.git my-supplement

git says that you cloned an empty repository. The new folder, my-supplement, is the site folder.

3. Make the site

In the R console, in the folder that holds my-supplement, run:

supplement::create_supplement("my-supplement", repo = "owner/name")

The function copies the template into the clone. It writes the repository into the GitHub link in _quarto.yml. It also writes the site’s GitHub Pages address, https://owner.github.io/name/, into the site’s README and into the guide for authors. If the folder already holds a file that the template writes, the function stops and writes nothing.

4. Render the site

In a terminal, in the site folder, run:

quarto render

The first render writes .gitignore and README.md, the page for the people who read the site’s repository. The guide for authors is GUIDE.md. The render also writes the site into docs/, the folder that GitHub Pages serves.

5. Commit and push

In a terminal, in the site folder, run:

git add -A
git commit -m "Start the site"
git push -u origin HEAD

HEAD pushes the branch that you are on. To see its name, run git branch --show-current. You need that name in the next step.

If git asks who you are, give it your name and email address, then run the commit again:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

If the push asks for a password, GitHub refuses it. Sign in with gh instead, let git use that sign-in, and run the push again:

gh auth login
gh auth setup-git
git push -u origin HEAD

6. Serve the site with GitHub Pages

On GitHub, open the repository’s Settings tab and click Pages. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch. Select the branch that you pushed and the /docs folder, and click Save. GitHub’s page Configuring a publishing source for your GitHub Pages site shows these settings.

The site is at https://owner.github.io/name/, with the owner in lowercase. For a repository named owner.github.io, the site is at https://owner.github.io/.

7. Turn on Zenodo for the repository

Do this step before your first release. Zenodo archives the new releases of a repository that has its switch on.

  1. Link your Zenodo account to GitHub. On Zenodo, open the profile menu, choose Linked accounts, and click Connect next to GitHub. If you signed up for Zenodo with GitHub, the accounts are already linked. Zenodo’s page Linking accounts shows these settings.
  2. Turn on the switch for the repository. On Zenodo, open the profile menu and choose GitHub. Click Sync now, find the repository, and turn on its switch. Zenodo’s page Enable a repository shows these settings.

8. Replace the template placeholders

The template holds example values. A release stops while any value in items 1 to 4 is in place. Items 5 and 6 do not stop a release, but visitors to the site or the repository see them. In the site folder:

  1. In _supplement.yml, write the paper title, the citation, the contact, and the authors. Leave version and the values under zenodo empty.
  2. In index.qmd, delete the box “Before your first commit”.
  3. In LICENSE.md and LICENSE-CC-BY.md, replace YEAR AUTHORS with the year and the authors.
  4. Replace the example report and data. Add your own with supplement::add_report() and supplement::add_data(). Then delete analyses/example.qmd, its stored output in _freeze/analyses/example/, and its item in the Analyses menu of _quarto.yml. Delete data/example.csv and its entry under data in _supplement.yml.
  5. Delete the example’s figure, figures/bootstrap-means.png. For a site with no figures of its own, also leave out figures from the git add command in the last part of this guide.
  6. In README.md, replace the example citation under the title with the paper’s citation.

Then, in a terminal in the site folder, render the whole site:

quarto render

In the R console, in the site folder, look for problems:

supplement::check_supplement()

Fix each problem that it prints, render again, and run it again. To also test the web addresses on the site’s pages, which needs a network, run supplement::check_supplement(web_links = TRUE). A row from that test can come from a site that you do not control, such as one that is down. release_supplement() does not run this test, so its rows do not stop a release.

When the check finds no problem, commit and push in a terminal in the site folder:

git add -A
git commit -m "Add the paper and the reports"
git push

9. Make the first release

In the R console, in the site folder, run:

supplement::release_supplement("major")

The function runs check_supplement() and stops if it finds a problem. Then it sets the site version to 1.0.0, writes CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json, and prints the commands that make the release. It runs none of them. Run the printed commands in a terminal in the site folder. The last command, gh release create, makes the GitHub release. If gh asks you to run gh auth login, run it, then run gh release create again.

10. Add the DOIs and render again

After Zenodo archives the release, its Zenodo record has a DOI. In _supplement.yml, under zenodo, write that DOI as version-doi and the address of the record page as archive-url. Zenodo also gives a concept DOI, which names every release of the repository. If you write it as concept-doi, the badge uses it when version-doi is empty. Write each DOI in the form 10.5281/zenodo.1234567.

In the R console, in the site folder, write the DOI into CITATION.cff:

supplement::write_citation(overwrite = TRUE)

Then, in a terminal in the site folder, render the site and push it:

quarto render
git add -A
git commit -m "Add the Zenodo DOIs"
git push

The home page now shows the DOI badge and the download link.

Render again after a report changes

Quarto stores the output of each report in _freeze/, and a full render reuses that output. A full render does not run a report again after you change it. So after a report changes, do these steps in a terminal in the site folder, with the report’s data in place:

  1. Render that report by name. This runs its code again.
  2. Render the whole site.
  3. Commit the changed report with _freeze/, docs/, and figures/, and push.

For a report in analyses/models.qmd, the commands are:

quarto render analyses/models.qmd
quarto render
git add analyses/models.qmd _freeze docs figures
git commit -m "Update the models report"
git push

When a path is missing from disk and git tracks no file under it, git add stops and stages nothing. So for a site with no figures/ folder, leave out figures.
